You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF nominal).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at nominal: low, so diode drops matter.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 2 of 12.

RESULTS OF YOUR PREVIOUS ROUND:

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a load RL from a piezo energy harvester.
    *   Requirements:
        *   $v_{avg} \ge 1.8\text{ V}$ (settled)
        *   $v_{max} \le 3.6\text{ V}$
        *   $v_{pp} \le 0.05\text{ V}$ (ripple)
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{ s}$ (startup)
        *   $dv \le 0.02\text{ V}$ (settled stability)
    *   Operating Conditions: S1 (Nominal), S2 (Heavy load), S3 (Strong exc, light load), S4 (Weak exc), S5 (Low freq), S6 (Hot, Cp+20%).
    *   Piezo: Current source $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$ || $C_p$ || $20\text{ M}\Omega$.
    *   Previous attempt (SSHI_FBR_Zener):
        *   Connectivity: Full bridge rectifier (FBR) + Zener clamp + an inductor-switch (SSHI-like) for inversion.
        *   Results: $v_{avg}$ and $v_{max}$ are generally okay (thanks to the Zener), but ripple is too high, and it's not settling (drifting). Startup is too slow on S4.
        *   The "settled" failure ($dv > 0.02\text{ V}$) and "ripple" failure ($v_{pp} > 0.05\text{ V}$) indicate that the output capacitor $C_{out}$ is likely too small for the ripple but too large for the startup time, *or* more likely, the system is still charging/discharging because the power delivered is too close to the power consumed, creating a very long time constant.

    *   The SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor) part (L1, S1, G1) is designed to flip the voltage across $C_p$ at the peaks, increasing the extracted energy.
    *   In the provided SSHI_FBR_Zener:
        *   FBR: D1-D4.
        *   Zener: DZ1.
        *   SSHI: L1 (pzp to n1), S1 (n1 to pzn).
        *   This is a "parallel" SSHI structure. The FBR is always there, and the switch periodically shorts the piezo through an inductor.
    *   Wait, the "settled" and "ripple" failures are severe. $v_{pp}$ is $344\text{ mV}$ on S5. $dv$ is $0.35\text{ V}$.
    *   The time constant $\tau = R_L \cdot C_{out}$ for $C_{out} = 4.7\text{ }\mu\text{F}$ and $R_L = 150\text{ k}\Omega$ (S2) is $0.705\text{ s}$. Since the simulation only runs for $0.8\text{ s}$, it's barely reaching steady state.
    *   To fix the "settled" failure, we need a faster response (smaller $C_{out}$) or more power. But smaller $C_{out}$ increases ripple.
    *   To fix "ripple", we need larger $C_{out}$.
    *   This is a classic tradeoff. However, the $dv$ failure suggests we aren't reaching steady state. The "startup" failure on S4 ($t_{up} = 0.529\text{ s}$) also suggests $C_{out}$ might be too large for the weak excitation of S4.

    *   Standard SSHI typically uses a switch to flip $C_p$ voltage *before* rectification.
    *   The current design has FBR and SSHI in parallel. Let's try a more integrated SSHI approach.
    *   Alternatively, maybe the Zener is too aggressive? No, it's at $3.3\text{ V}$, which is good for $v_{max} \le 3.6\text{ V}$.
    *   What about a Synchronous Rectifier (active bridge)? We only have 2 SYNC controllers and 4 switches. We could replace two diodes with switches, but that's complex.
    *   Let's look at the "ripple" again. $v_{pp}$ is high. Maybe the FBR is losing too much voltage? DSCH diodes have low drop, but at $1.8\text{ V}$ output, the piezo voltage must reach $1.8 + 0.25 = 2.05\text{ V}$.
    *   The open-circuit voltage $V_{oc} = I_p / (2\pi f C_p)$. For S4 (weak), $I_p = 30\text{ }\mu\text{A}, f=100, C_p=25\text{nF} \Rightarrow V_{oc} = 30\text{e-6} / (2\pi \cdot 100 \cdot 25\text{e-9}) \approx 19.1\text{ V}$.
    *   Wait, the prompt says $V_{oc}$ is "about $3.2\text{ V}$ at nominal". Let me re-calculate. $50\text{e-6} / (2\pi \cdot 100 \cdot 25\text{e-9}) \approx 31.8\text{ V}$.
    *   Wait, is the piezo model $I_p \sin(\omega t)$ in parallel with $C_p$? Yes.
    *   If the prompt says $V_{oc} \approx 3.2\text{ V}$, maybe my formula is wrong or I'm misreading. "Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is $Ip/(2\pi f Cp)$, about $3.2\text{ V}$ at nominal".
    *   Let's check the math again: $50\text{e-6} / (2 \cdot 3.14 \cdot 100 \cdot 25\text{e-9}) = 50\text{e-6} / 1.57\text{e-5} = 3.184\text{ V}$. Ah, my power of 10 was wrong. It's $3.18\text{ V}$.
    *   Okay, so $V_{oc}$ is very low. With $V_{oc} \approx 3.2\text{ V}$, a full bridge (2 diode drops $\approx 0.5\text{ V}$) is a huge loss.
    *   A half-bridge or a switch-based rectifier would be better. But we are limited to 4 switches.

    *   The current design uses a full bridge. For $V_{oc} = 3.2\text{ V}$, we are losing significant energy.
    *   Let's try a "Synchronous" approach for rectification or a charge pump? No, too many components.
    *   What if we use a "half-bridge" with a capacitor? Not possible with a single-ended piezo.
    *   Let's try a "Switch-Capacitor" or a "Voltage Doubler"? No, that might exceed $v_{max}$.
    *   Wait, look at the SSHI_FBR_Zener result: it *did* pass $v_{avg}$ and $v_{max}$ for most cases. The main issues are ripple and settling.
    *   The ripple is $v_{pp}$. $v_{pp} \approx \Delta Q / C_{out}$. $\Delta Q$ is the charge delivered per cycle.
    *   If we can't increase $C_{out}$ (due to startup/settling), we must reduce the charge pulses or increase the frequency of delivery.
    *   Wait, if $V_{oc}$ is so low, maybe we should use a simpler rectifier?
    *   The FBR is: `D1: pzp -> out`, `D2: pzn -> out`, `D3: 0 -> pzp`, `D4: 0 -> pzn`. This is a standard bridge.
    *   What if we use a "synchronous rectifier" using the SYNC switches?
    *   For $V_{oc} = 3.2\text{ V}$, we need every millivolt.
    *   Let's try a "Synchronous SSHI" where the switch not only flips the voltage but also assists in the transfer.
    *   Actually, let's consider the "Cold Start" ($t_{up}$). The current SSHI_FBR_Zener has a $t_{up}$ of $0.529\text{ s}$ for S4. $C_{out} = 4.7\text{ }\mu\text{F}$ is likely too large.
    *   If we reduce $C_{out}$ to $1\text{ }\mu\text{F}$:
        *   $t_{up}$ will decrease (Good).
        *   $dv$ (settling) will decrease (Good).
        *   $v_{pp}$ (ripple) will increase (Bad).
    *   How to reduce ripple without increasing $C_{out}$?
        *   The ripple is caused by the discrete nature of the energy delivery. In a full bridge, we deliver charge twice per period.
        *   Is there a way to smooth the current?
        *   Maybe an LC filter? We have inductors. An L-C filter after the rectifier could work.
        *   Proposed structure: Piezo $\to$ FBR $\to$ Inductor L_filter $\to$ $C_{out}$.
        *   Wait, the L-C filter would be: FBR nodes $\to$ $L_{filt}$ $\to$ node "out". This would significantly reduce ripple.

    *   Current: FBR $\to$ $C_{out}$.
    *   New: FBR $\to$ $L_{filt} \to C_{out}$.
    *   Wait, a simple L-C filter on a rectifier output:
        The rectifier outputs pulses. The inductor $L_{filt}$ smooths the current.
        Circuit:
        - D1, D2, D3, D4 (Full Bridge)
        - $L_{filt}$ from "out_rect" to "out"
        - $C_{out}$ from "out" to "0"
        - $DZ1$ (Zener) from "out" to "0"
    *   But wait, if I put $L_{filt}$ between the rectifier and $C_{out}$, the rectifier must be able to push current through the inductor.
    *   Actually, a more common way to reduce ripple is a larger $C_{out}$, but we already saw that hurts settling and startup.
    *   What if we use a "Synchronous Rectifier" using the switches?
        S1: pzp to out, S2: pzn to out... but we only have 4 switches and they are controlled by SYNC.
        SYNC closes for `ton` at the peaks.
        If we use a SYNC switch to connect the piezo to the output at the peaks, it's like a sampled-data system.
    *   Let's try a different SSHI topology. The "Parallel SSHI" we used is:
        Piezo || FBR || (L1 + S1).
        This flips $V_{Cp}$ but still relies on FBR for delivery.
    *   What if we use a "Series SSHI" or just a better-tuned FBR?
        The reference FBR failed S2 (heavy load) and S4 (weak). The SSHI_FBR_Zener *passed* $v_{avg}$ for S2 and S4! This means the SSHI part is working to increase the power.
    *   So the power is sufficient. The problem is purely the output filter ($C_{out}$).
    *   If $C_{out}$ is too small $\to$ ripple. If $C_{out}$ is too large $\to$ settling/startup.
    *   Is there a way to have a "fast" startup and "low" ripple?
        Yes, a smaller $C_{out}$ but with a more continuous current.
    *   Wait, the $dv$ (settled) is $|mean(0.7-0.8) - mean(0.6-0.7)|$.
        If the output is still charging slowly, $dv$ will be large.
        If the power delivered $P_{in}$ is very close to $P_{load}$, the approach to steady state is very slow.
        $P_{in} \approx P_{load} + \frac{C_{out} \Delta V}{\Delta t}$.
        If $P_{in} - P_{load}$ is small, $\Delta V$ is small and the time constant is huge.
        The SSHI_FBR_Zener is delivering $55.8\text{ }\mu\text{W}$ for S2, while the load needs $V^2/R_L = 2.89^2 / 150\text{k} \approx 55.6\text{ }\mu\text{W}$.
        It's *barely* enough! That's why it's not settling.
    *   To fix "settled", we need more power. To get more power, we need a more efficient rectifier.
    *   A full bridge of DSCH diodes has $\approx 0.5\text{ V}$ drop.
    *   What if we use a "Half-Bridge" rectifier?
        A half-bridge requires a capacitor in series with the piezo or a center-tap. We don't have a center-tap.
        A "Charge Pump" or "Voltage Doubler" could work?
        Example: $C_1$ from pzn to 0, D1 from pzn to n1, D2 from pzp to n1... no.
    *   Let's try a "Synchronous Rectifier" (SR).
        Instead of D1, D2, D3, D4, we use switches.
        But SYNC switches are only closed for `ton` (max $1\text{ ms}$).
        $1\text{ ms}$ at $100\text{ Hz}$ is $1/100$ of the period. That's not a rectifier; that's a sampler.
    *   Wait! The SYNC controller can have `edges: "both"`.
        If we use a SYNC switch to "flip" the voltage and then let the diodes do the rectifying, that's what we did.
        What if we use the inductor to *boost* the voltage?
        A boost converter: $L$ in series with the source, a switch to ground, and a diode to the output.
        Piezo (pzp-pzn) $\to$ $L_{boost}$ $\to$ node `sw`.
        Switch S1 from `sw` to `0`.
        Diode D1 from `sw` to `out`.
        This is a boost converter. When S1 is closed, $L_{boost}$ charges. When S1 opens, the energy is pushed to `out`.
        But the piezo is an AC source. We'd need a bridge first or a more complex setup.

    *   Let's reconsider the SSHI. The current SSHI structure (L1 and S1 in parallel with the piezo) is a "voltage flipper".
        It's known to increase the power extracted from a piezo.
        If the power is still too low (making it not settle), we need to be more efficient.
        Maybe we can replace the FBR with a "Half-Bridge Rectifier" using a "flying capacitor"?
        Or a "Dickson Charge Pump"?
        Wait, the simplest way to get more power than an FBR is a "Synchronous Rectifier". Since we can't do a full SR, maybe a "half-synchronous" one?
        Or, maybe just use the inductor more effectively.

    *   Let's try a "Boost-based" harvester.
        A common topology is the "Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction" (SECE).
        SECE uses a switch to connect the piezo to an inductor, then a switch to connect the inductor to the load.
        But that requires 2 switches and precise timing.
        We have 2 SYNC controllers.
        G1: closes S1 at the peaks.
